## The browser lab and the workspace {#what-we-use-today .smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**The browser lab**

- One web page, in which R runs **inside the browser**
- Nothing to install, and the data are already in place
- Each task is a cell that you edit and run, with hints and a solution beneath it
- The page that I drive on the shared screen, and the one in which the day runs
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**The workspace, if you installed it**

- The folder you downloaded, opened in your IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.)
- The same tasks, data and helpers, in a report that Quarto renders
- The copy of the work that you keep and take home
- No git, no cloning and no configuration – it is a folder of files
:::
:::
::::

::: {.urlbox .fragment}
[{{< var site-url >}}cases/eu-frames/lab.html]({{< var site-url >}}cases/eu-frames/lab.html)
:::

::: notes
This is what you will work in today. The browser lab is one web page, and R itself runs inside your browser, so there is nothing to install and nothing to break, and the data are already there. Each task is a cell: you fill a gap or change a line, press Run Code, and the output appears beneath it, with hints and a worked solution under every exercise. That is the page I will drive on the shared screen. If you installed R and an IDE and downloaded the workspace, it holds the same tasks, the same data and the same helper functions, as a report that you render. It is also the copy that you keep, because the browser lab forgets everything when you reload it. The address of the lab is on the slide and in the chat.
:::

## What the tools cannot do {.smaller}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
A perfectly reproducible pipeline can be a perfectly reproducible answer to **a question you never stated**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
None of this software will tell you what your estimand is, whether your controls belong in the model, or whether the association you found means what you think it means.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Tooling is the **cheap** half of the problem, because it can be learned. **The expensive half is the question that the analysis is meant to answer.**
:::
::::

::: notes
All of this software is worth having, but a perfectly reproducible pipeline can be a perfectly reproducible answer to a question you never stated. None of this software will tell you what your estimand is, whether the variables you put in the model belong there, or whether the association you found means what you think it means. Tooling is the cheap half of the problem, in the sense that it can be solved by learning things. The expensive half starts from a question that every quantitative study has to answer, namely what exactly you are trying to estimate, and a good deal of what follows is about that question. First, though, you need a setup that works.
:::
